title: Lists
description: Store many values in order inside a single variable, then read and change them.

content.text: So far, every variable held **one** value. A list is one variable that holds many values, kept in order like carriages on a train.

parts.label: items
parts.note: The values, separated by commas. Strings, numbers, or a mix of both.

parts.label: close
parts.note: The closing bracket ends the list.

content.value:
toys = ["Lego", "Teddy Bear", "Action Figure"]
scores = [10, 25, 3]
print(toys)
print(len(toys))
content.caption: `len()` tells you how many items the list holds.
Each list is still just one box, holding many values.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `len()` counts the items. There are four numbers in the list.

items: Each item has a position number called its **index**.
Python starts counting at **0**: the first item is index `0`, the second is index `1`.
The last item is always at `len(toys) - 1`.
Negative indexes count back from the end: `toys[-1]` is the last item.

items.title: Counting from the front
items.code:
toys[0]   # Lego
toys[1]   # Teddy Bear
toys[2]   # Action Figure

items.title: Counting from the back
items.code:
toys[-1]  # Action Figure
toys[-2]  # Teddy Bear
toys[-3]  # Lego

content.title: Indexes for toys
content.caption: Ask for an index that does not exist and Python stops with an `IndexError`. Three items means the only valid indexes are `0`, `1` and `2`. Index `3` is already past the end.

content.value:
toys = ["Lego", "Teddy Bear", "Action Figure"]
print(toys[0])
print(toys[2])
print(toys[-1])
Try it in the lab below: read each index, then try one past the end.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: Counting starts at 0: `red` is index 0, `blue` is index 1.

items.sub: Adds one item to the end.
Replaces whatever was in that slot.

content.title: A list can change after you make it

content.code:
toys = ["Lego", "Teddy Bear"]
toys.append("Water Gun")
toys[0] = "Robot"
toys.pop()
print(toys)

steps.note: `.append()` adds `"Water Gun"` to the end. Now there are three items.
Index `0` is the first slot. `"Lego"` is replaced by `"Robot"`.
Print the list as it is now.

content.title: Watch the list change
content.outro: Same variable the whole time. Only the items inside changed.

content.value: `.append()` changes the list in place and hands nothing back. Writing `toys = toys.append("Ball")` throws the list away and leaves you with `None`. Call it on its own line.
content.title: append gives nothing back

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: Lines run in order. `.pop()` removes the last item, `3`, leaving `[1, 2]`. Then `.append(4)` adds `4` to the end.

items: In Module 3 your `for` loops counted through numbers from `range()`.
A `for` loop can walk straight through a list instead, one item at a time.
No indexes needed, and it works however long the list is.

steps.note: The loop takes the first item and puts it in `toy`.
Back to the top: the next item.
After this, there are no items left, so the loop ends.

content.title: Watch the loop walk the list

content.value: One list plus one loop replaces however many copied print lines you would otherwise write. Adding a fourth toy needs no new code at all.
content.title: Why lists and loops go together

content.question: How many times does the body of this loop run?
content.explain: The loop runs once per item, and the list has four items.

editorCode:
shopping = ["Apples", "Cookies", "Milk"]
shopping.append("Juice")

print("First item:", shopping[0])
print("Items:", len(shopping))

for item in shopping:
    print("-", item)

quiz.question: What index does the first item in a list have?
quiz.explain: Python counts from 0, so the first item is at index 0 and the second at index 1.

quiz.question: A list has 4 items. Which index gives the LAST one?
quiz.explain: Four items use the indexes 0, 1, 2, 3. The last index is always the length minus one, so index 4 would be an IndexError.

quiz.question: Which line adds 'Ball' to the end of a list called toys?
quiz.explain: .append() puts one item on the end. Lists have no .add(), and .insert() needs a position as well as the item.
